children: Sovereign total return swaps could increase the pain for bondholders in a restructuring, ratings agency Fitch said on Tuesday.
Total return swaps are derivative contracts that can be used by governments to raise financing outside traditional bond markets, often using existing assets as collateral.

The ratings agency warned that the existing sovereign debt architecture, including the Common Framework, "is not yet well equipped to address" uncertainties around how they would be treated in a restructuring.
Senegal said last week that it would rework its debt under an "enhanced" Common Framework process.
Angola, Nigeria and Colombia have used such instruments to raise hard-currency cash over the past several years.
Fitch said that despite criticism from multilateral lenders, "the interest in these instruments remains significant".

Fitch said countries have an incentive to avoid default on total return swaps backed by local currency bonds "at any cost" because such an event could "transmit stress directly into the domestic financial system."

Fitch said creditors could recover up to 100% if a country repays or unwinds its TRS before a restructuring, or if the counterparty sells the underlying collateral after the process begins, because they would be repaid in cash or recover value from bonds they already hold rather than take part in any negotiated haircut.

"This comes at the direct expense of conventional bondholders," Fitch said, as they are part of a smaller pool of creditors taking losses and the country subsequently has fewer assets at its disposal.
The IMF has told Reuters that in Senegal’s case, total return swaps transactions involving external creditors are currently classified as external debt.
Fitch previously warned that total return swaps could increase concerns over transparency and structural risk.

Dakar said that as of December 2025, it had raised 721 billion CFA francs ($1.27 billion) in net financing from total return swaps in transactions backed by CFA franc-denominated bonds, though the full terms of the arrangements are not publicly known.
